questions.q: What is the difference between an SLO and an SLA?
options: There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
An SLO is the internal target you engineer to; an SLA is a contractual promise with consequences, usually set looser than the SLO
An SLA only applies to latency, while an SLO only applies to availability
An SLO is measured by customers; an SLA is measured by engineers
questions.explain: An SLO is the internal target a team holds itself to. An SLA is a contract with consequences attached, deliberately set looser so there's margin between what you promise externally and what you target internally.

questions.q: Why do ML platforms report latency as p50/p95/p99 instead of a single average?
options: Percentiles are easier to calculate than an average
An average can look healthy while a meaningful fraction of requests have a terrible experience, which percentiles expose
Averages are not supported by monitoring tools
p50/p95/p99 only matter for batch-scored models, not real-time ones
questions.explain: A handful of slow requests (cold starts, slow feature lookups) can be invisible in an average while clearly showing up at p95 or p99, which is why platforms track percentiles separately.

questions.q: What does a feature freshness SLO guard against that a normal availability SLO would miss entirely?
options: A model endpoint returning HTTP 500 errors
A model serving requests successfully and quickly while reading quietly stale feature data, degrading decisions without throwing any error
A deployment pipeline running too slowly
A user submitting invalid input to a prediction endpoint
questions.explain: Stale features can make a model's decisions worse while every other signal — errors, latency — looks completely normal. Freshness is the SLO type that catches this.

questions.q: In the SRE error-budget model, what happens as a team's error budget becomes exhausted?
options: Nothing changes — the error budget is purely informational
The team is required to immediately roll back every recent deployment
Deployments typically slow down, require manual approval, or freeze for non-critical changes until the budget resets
The SLO target is automatically loosened to match actual performance
questions.explain: An exhausted error budget is meant to change behavior: risky or non-critical deployments pause so the team can focus on reliability until the budget recovers.

questions.q: Why do platform teams write SLOs as versioned config files rather than keeping them only in a slide deck or wiki page?
options: Config files render faster in a browser
So the SLOs live next to the service they govern and can feed directly into alerting and deployment-approval automation
Because SLAs legally require a YAML format
Slide decks cannot contain percentages
questions.explain: Keeping SLOs as config lets them drive real automation — alerting thresholds and deployment approval gates — instead of being a static document nobody checks against.
